messages.content: I want to develop unsupervised speech recognition accent adaptation that separates pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation without sacrificing existing accents. What exactly does that goal require?

It requires adaptation to respond to pronunciation differences associated with an unseen accent without treating differences between speakers or recording channels as if they were accent changes. The adaptation must use only unlabeled adaptation speech. It also has two quantitative requirements: reduce unseen-accent word error rate (WER) by at least 15% relative to a frozen recognizer, and limit increases in existing-accent WER to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels. Those are targets for the work, not reported results.
Can you clarify the 15% requirement? Is that a drop of 15 WER percentage points?

No. It is a relative reduction of at least 15% compared with the frozen recognizer’s unseen-accent WER. If that baseline WER is B, the target is an adapted unseen-accent WER no greater than 0.85 × B. The requirement does not specify a baseline WER value, so it does not imply a fixed percentage-point reduction.
And the one-point limit uses the same kind of relative calculation?

No. That limit is expressed in percentage points of WER: existing-accent WER may increase by no more than one percentage point. It is not a one-percent relative increase. The two thresholds use different units, and keeping that distinction matters when interpreting whether the goal has been met.
When I say ‘without sacrificing existing accents,’ do I mean their WER cannot rise at all?

The stated quantitative requirement allows an increase of up to one percentage point in existing-accent WER. So ‘without sacrificing existing accents’ should be read alongside that explicit tolerance, rather than as an absolute requirement of zero increase.
Why distinguish pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation here?

They are different sources of variation in speech. The desired adaptation concerns pronunciation shifts associated with an accent. A change in speaker or channel may also change what the recognizer receives, but the goal is not to mistake those changes for the pronunciation shift it is meant to address. The distinction matters both for improving recognition of the unseen accent and for retaining recognition of existing accents.
Does ‘independently varying speakers and channels’ mean that I can assume a particular speaker always uses a particular channel?

No. The condition explicitly says speakers and channels vary independently. The existing-accent WER limit must hold under that condition, rather than relying on a fixed association between a speaker and a channel.
How does the unlabeled-speech condition constrain the goal?

The adaptation speech cannot supply word-level answers as labels. The required unseen-accent improvement must be obtained using only unlabeled adaptation speech, rather than labeled adaptation examples. That describes what information is available for adaptation; it does not, by itself, specify an adaptation method.
Is the frozen recognizer the system I am trying to beat on the unseen accent?

Yes. The frozen recognizer is the explicit comparison for the unseen-accent requirement. The adapted recognizer’s unseen-accent WER must be at least 15% lower relative to that frozen-recognizer WER, while the existing-accent WER increase remains within the separately stated one-percentage-point limit.
Could an apparent unseen-accent improvement be enough if it came with a larger existing-accent WER increase?

It would not satisfy the full goal. The unseen-accent reduction and the existing-accent limit are simultaneous requirements. Meeting the at-least-15% relative reduction does not waive the one-percentage-point ceiling on existing-accent WER increases.
Do these requirements tell us which adaptation technique to use?

No. They define the objective, the allowed adaptation information, the comparison for unseen-accent WER, and the constraint on existing-accent WER under independently varying speakers and channels. They do not specify an architecture, training procedure, dataset, or completed experiment.
So the central difficulty is to improve recognition of pronunciation differences without letting other variation drive the adaptation?

That captures it. More precisely, the goal is unsupervised accent adaptation that separates pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation, achieves at least a 15% relative unseen-accent WER reduction against the frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech, and keeps existing-accent WER increases to at most one percentage point when speakers and channels vary independently.
What approach would you propose for that goal?

I would propose training accent-gated phoneme residual adapters from confidence-filtered pseudo-labels, with adversarial speaker/channel disentanglement and a frozen-recognizer fallback for existing accents. Each part addresses a different concern in the goal: adapting pronunciation, avoiding confusion with speaker and channel variation, and protecting performance on existing accents. It is a proposal, not a demonstrated result.
Can you unpack ‘accent-gated phoneme residual adapters’?

The proposed adapters are intended to make pronunciation-related adjustments at the phoneme level, rather than replacing the recognizer outright. ‘Residual’ describes an adjustment to the existing recognition path, and ‘accent-gated’ means the use of that adjustment is conditioned on the accent-related path being appropriate. The proposal does not specify the gate’s implementation or establish how reliably it will distinguish accents.
Why make the adapters residual instead of treating adaptation as an entirely new recognizer?

Within this proposal, the residual form frames adaptation as a modification to an existing recognizer, while leaving room for its unchanged behavior to matter. That fits the requirement to improve unseen-accent WER without sacrificing existing accents. It does not, on its own, guarantee either WER requirement.
Does ‘phoneme’ mean the adaptation is specifically aimed at pronunciation shifts?

Yes, that is the intent of phoneme residual adapters here: to focus the adjustment on pronunciation-related differences. The separate disentanglement component addresses the risk that speaker or channel differences could be confused with those pronunciation shifts.
How can training use pseudo-labels if the adaptation speech is supposed to be unlabeled?

Pseudo-labels are tentative labels produced without supplied ground-truth labels for the adaptation speech. Using them does not change the condition that the adaptation speech is unlabeled. The proposal further specifies confidence filtering, so training would draw on pseudo-labels that pass a confidence criterion rather than treating every tentative label as equally suitable. It does not specify how that criterion is set.
Should I interpret confidence-filtered as meaning the retained pseudo-labels are correct?

No. Filtering by confidence is a proposed way to limit reliance on less-confident pseudo-labels; confidence is not proof of correctness. The approach still has to contend with errors in tentative labels, and the proposal does not claim that filtering eliminates them.
What is the adversarial speaker/channel disentanglement meant to do?

It is meant to discourage the adaptation from using speaker and channel variation as a substitute for accent-related pronunciation information. That directly serves the goal of separating pronunciation shifts from those other sources of variation. ‘Adversarial’ names the proposed disentanglement approach; the node does not specify a particular adversarial objective or claim that perfect separation has been achieved.
If a recording sounds different because of the channel, would this proposal simply call that a new accent?

It is designed not to. Speaker/channel disentanglement is included precisely because a difference in recording channel should not automatically be treated as a pronunciation shift. Whether the proposed approach succeeds at making that distinction is an open performance question, not something established by the proposal.
What role does the frozen-recognizer fallback play for existing accents?

The proposed fallback preserves access to the frozen recognizer for existing accents rather than requiring every case to rely on the adapted path. Its purpose is to help protect existing-accent recognition while pursuing an unseen-accent improvement. The proposal does not establish that fallback will always be invoked appropriately or that it will, by itself, hold the WER increase within the required limit.
Is the fallback also the comparison baseline for the unseen-accent target?

The frozen recognizer is the stated baseline for the unseen-accent WER comparison, and the proposal also uses it as a fallback for existing accents. Those roles are related but distinct: the target is at least a 15% relative reduction in unseen-accent WER against the frozen recognizer, while the fallback is part of the proposed way to protect existing-accent performance.
Could we say that using the fallback already satisfies the existing-accent requirement?

Not yet. The requirement is that existing-accent WER increases be limited to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels. Including a frozen-recognizer fallback is a proposed safeguard, not evidence that the resulting behavior meets that limit under those conditions.
And the accent gate is intended to decide when the residual adaptation is relevant?

That is the intended role of accent gating in this proposal. It provides a way to condition use of the phoneme residual adjustment on accent relevance, while the frozen-recognizer fallback is available for existing accents. The proposal does not specify a decision rule for the gate, so it would be premature to claim that it reliably makes that distinction.
Do the gate and the disentanglement component solve the same problem?

They have complementary aims. Accent gating concerns when the pronunciation-oriented adjustment is applied. Adversarial speaker/channel disentanglement concerns what kinds of variation the adaptation learns to rely on. Both support the broader aim of adapting to pronunciation shifts without confusing them with speaker or channel changes, but neither is stated as a proven solution.
What would count as success for this proposal, rather than just a plausible design?

It would need to meet the original requirements: using only unlabeled adaptation speech, achieve at least a 15% relative reduction in unseen-accent WER compared with the frozen recognizer, while limiting existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point when speakers and channels vary independently. The proposed components describe how to pursue those requirements; they are not themselves measurements of success.
So I should present this as a candidate method, not as an adaptation system that has already cleared the targets?

Exactly. The candidate method combines confidence-filtered pseudo-label training, accent-gated phoneme residual adapters, adversarial speaker/channel disentanglement, and frozen-recognizer fallback for existing accents. Its rationale aligns with the goal, but the proposal alone does not show that either WER threshold has been met.
Does a 0.85 pseudo-label confidence cutoff discard systematic vowel shifts needed to train the accent-gated phoneme residuals?

It might, but the cutoff alone does not tell us. If systematic vowel shifts cause the recognizer to assign lower confidence to the corresponding pseudo-labels, filtering at 0.85 could exclude precisely the pronunciation differences the residuals are meant to learn. If those labels remain sufficiently confident, they need not be excluded. This is a concern about the proposed training signal, not an established finding.
Why might a useful vowel shift end up with low pseudo-label confidence?

The recognizer may be less certain about speech that differs from the pronunciations it already handles well. In that case, a shifted vowel could be informative for accent adaptation while its tentative label falls below the confidence cutoff. But a systematic shift does not necessarily produce low confidence, so we cannot infer that this happens merely from the word ‘shift.’
So does 0.85 describe how much of the vowel-shift speech is retained?

No. It is a proposed confidence cutoff, not a retention rate. The proportion of relevant speech retained would depend on the confidence values assigned to its pseudo-labels. Knowing the cutoff is 0.85 does not tell us that proportion.
Would confidence filtering necessarily favor ordinary pronunciations over the shifted vowels?

Not necessarily. That is the possible selection bias the question raises: if shifted vowels receive lower confidence than other speech, the retained pseudo-labels could underrepresent them. But the question does not establish how confidence is distributed, so it does not establish that the bias occurs or how large it is.
Could the opposite problem happen—confident pseudo-labels for shifted vowels that are nevertheless wrong?

Yes, in principle. A confidence score is not a guarantee that a pseudo-label is correct. A 0.85 cutoff could retain confidently wrong labels as well as discard uncertain but useful ones. That is why neither passing nor failing the cutoff, by itself, tells us whether a pseudo-label supplies a good signal for learning a pronunciation shift.
If the filter does discard those examples, what would that mean for the phoneme residuals?

It would reduce the direct training signal from the discarded vowel-shift examples. If the residuals need those examples to learn the relevant pronunciation adjustment, that would be a problem for the proposed approach. The conditional matters: we do not yet know which examples are discarded or whether the retained speech provides enough relevant signal.
Does accent gating make the filtering concern go away?

No. Accent gating concerns when the phoneme residual adjustment is used; confidence filtering concerns which tentative labels are available to train it. A gate does not, merely by existing, restore pronunciation examples excluded by the filter.
And speaker/channel disentanglement is a separate issue?

Yes. Its proposed role is to keep speaker and channel variation from being mistaken for accent-related pronunciation variation. The 0.85-cutoff question is narrower: whether confidence filtering removes vowel-shift information needed by the phoneme residuals. Addressing one concern does not automatically resolve the other.
Would a systematic shift at least guarantee that enough examples survive, because it recurs?

No. Recurrence and retention are different. A shift could recur consistently yet still receive confidence below the cutoff each time; alternatively, recurring examples might pass it. ‘Systematic’ tells us the pronunciation difference is patterned, not what confidence the pseudo-labels receive.
Is it fair to say 0.85 is too strict, then?

That conclusion is not supported by the question alone. A 0.85 cutoff could discard needed shifted-vowel examples, but it could also retain them while filtering less reliable pseudo-labels. The unresolved issue is what happens to the pronunciation information the adapters need, not whether the number is inherently too strict.
What would I need to know to answer the question rather than just state the risk?

You would need to know whether pseudo-labels associated with the systematic vowel shifts fall below the 0.85 cutoff, and whether the retained labels still represent those shifts well enough to train the accent-gated phoneme residuals. The cutoff alone provides neither answer.
So the question is not whether pseudo-label confidence is useful at all, but whether this filtering removes the very accent evidence the method relies on?

Exactly. Confidence filtering is intended to avoid relying indiscriminately on tentative labels, while the residuals need information about pronunciation shifts. The question asks whether setting the cutoff at 0.85 creates a conflict between those aims for systematic vowel shifts. It identifies a possibility to resolve, not a demonstrated failure.

Here is my hypothesis: a 0.85 pseudo-label confidence cutoff excludes at least 40% of shifted-vowel frames, and phoneme-balanced inclusion down to 0.70 should reduce unseen-accent WER. How should I interpret it?

It makes two connected predictions. First, the 0.85 cutoff is hypothesized to filter out ≥40% of frames containing the shifted vowels. Second, including lower-confidence pseudo-labels down to 0.70 in a phoneme-balanced way is expected to improve unseen-accent word error rate (WER). Neither the exclusion rate nor the WER improvement is an observed result in this statement.
Is the ≥40% figure about all adaptation speech?

No. Its denominator is shifted-vowel frames, not all adaptation speech, all vowel frames, or all words. The hypothesis says that at least 40% of that specific set of frames is excluded by the 0.85 cutoff.
Does that mean at least 40% would come back if I lowered the cutoff to 0.70?

Not necessarily. The exclusion hypothesis does not say where the excluded frames’ confidence values fall. Some might be between 0.70 and 0.85, while others might be below 0.70. It would be inaccurate to equate the hypothesized ≥40% excluded at 0.85 with the proportion recoverable by including pseudo-labels down to 0.70.
Then what is the point of specifying 0.70?

It defines the proposed extension of inclusion: the hypothesis considers phoneme-balanced inclusion down to a 0.70 confidence level, rather than relying solely on the 0.85 cutoff. The predicted benefit is a reduction in unseen-accent WER. The statement does not quantify how many additional shifted-vowel frames that change would admit.
What does ‘phoneme-balanced’ add? Why not just say ‘lower the cutoff’?

‘Phoneme-balanced’ qualifies how the lower-confidence material would be included: the intention is to account for phoneme representation, rather than treating inclusion as simply accepting everything that meets a lower cutoff without regard to phoneme. The hypothesis does not give a specific balancing rule, so it should not be read as specifying exact numbers of examples or a particular implementation.
Are we saying those excluded frames are definitely the examples the residual adapters need?

No. The hypothesis connects their possible exclusion to the concern that useful vowel-shift information may be lost, but exclusion alone does not establish that every such frame has a correct pseudo-label or would help train the accent-gated phoneme residuals. The claim to examine is whether the proposed phoneme-balanced inclusion improves unseen-accent WER.
Could including lower-confidence pseudo-labels also introduce mistakes?

Yes. Lowering the inclusion boundary can admit tentative labels that are less certain, and confidence does not guarantee correctness at either threshold. That is an important qualification to the prediction: gaining potential information about shifted vowels does not automatically translate into lower WER.
Does ‘should reduce unseen-accent WER’ mean it should achieve our ≥15% relative improvement against the frozen recognizer?

No. This hypothesis predicts a reduction in unseen-accent WER from phoneme-balanced inclusion down to 0.70, but it states no size for that reduction and does not claim that the broader target—at least a 15% relative reduction versus the frozen recognizer—has been reached. It also does not establish the separate existing-accent WER limit.
What if the ≥40% exclusion prediction turns out to be right? Would the WER prediction follow automatically?

No. Confirming that many shifted-vowel frames are excluded at 0.85 would identify a potential loss of training information. It would not, by itself, show that inclusion down to 0.70 recovers enough useful frames, that their pseudo-labels are suitable, or that phoneme-balanced inclusion reduces unseen-accent WER. The two predictions are connected but distinct.
And if unseen-accent WER drops, can I assume the ≥40% estimate was right?

Not from the WER change alone. A reduction would speak to the predicted outcome, but it would not establish the stated exclusion fraction. The ≥40% figure is specifically about shifted-vowel frames filtered by the 0.85 cutoff; WER is a separate, word-level measure.
Is the 0.70 value itself claimed to be optimal?

No. The hypothesis proposes phoneme-balanced inclusion down to 0.70 and predicts that it should reduce unseen-accent WER. It does not claim that 0.70 is optimal, nor does it compare that value with other possible cutoffs.
How should I phrase the idea without making it sound like a completed finding?

You could say: ‘We hypothesize that a 0.85 pseudo-label confidence cutoff excludes at least 40% of shifted-vowel frames, and that phoneme-balanced inclusion down to 0.70 will reduce unseen-accent WER.’ That preserves the frame-level exclusion threshold and the predicted WER effect while making clear that both remain hypotheses.

I want to compare 0.85 filtering with phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling on unlabeled AccentShift-12, measuring shifted-vowel retention and speaker/channel-stratified unseen- and existing-accent WER. Does that address the cutoff question?

Yes, as a plan. Comparing those two ways of selecting pseudo-labels would address whether the 0.85 filter retains less shifted-vowel information than phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling. Measuring unseen-accent WER would address the predicted recognition benefit, while existing-accent WER stratified by speaker and channel would keep the protection requirement in view. The comparison has not yet produced a result.
What is the distinction between 0.85 filtering and phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling in this comparison?

The first condition filters pseudo-labels at a confidence cutoff of 0.85. The second proposes sampling down to 0.70 while accounting for phoneme balance. It is not merely an instruction to accept every pseudo-label above 0.70 indiscriminately. The plan names the two conditions but does not specify the balancing procedure.
Is AccentShift-12 being used as labeled adaptation data?

No. The plan specifies unlabeled AccentShift-12 for the comparison. That is consistent with using pseudo-labels rather than supplied labels for adaptation. It does not specify every detail of how the WER measurements or the shifted-vowel retention measurement will be obtained.
When we say ‘shifted-vowel retention,’ what are we trying to learn?

We are trying to learn how much of the relevant shifted-vowel material remains available under each pseudo-label selection condition. That speaks directly to the concern that a 0.85 cutoff might discard vowel shifts needed by the accent-gated phoneme residuals. Retention is about which material is kept; it is not itself a measure of whether recognition improves.
So if 0.70 sampling retains more shifted-vowel frames, can I conclude that unseen-accent WER will fall?

No. More retention would answer part of the selection question, but the retained pseudo-labels might still be wrong or unhelpful. The plan measures unseen-accent WER separately because a change in retained frames does not guarantee a recognition benefit.
How does this speak to my hypothesis that the 0.85 cutoff excludes at least 40% of shifted-vowel frames?

The shifted-vowel retention measurement can bear on that specific prediction. The ≥40% figure concerns the fraction of shifted-vowel frames excluded at 0.85, not the fraction of all adaptation speech excluded. The plan does not yet tell us what that fraction is, or how many excluded frames phoneme-balanced sampling down to 0.70 would recover.
Why measure WER for existing accents if the cutoff question is about shifted vowels in an unseen accent?

Because the broader goal requires an unseen-accent improvement without an existing-accent WER increase greater than one percentage point. A selection change that helps the unseen accent could still affect existing-accent recognition. Measuring both makes it possible to examine that trade-off rather than judging the 0.70 condition on unseen-accent WER alone.
What does speaker/channel-stratified WER add?

It asks for the unseen- and existing-accent WER measurements to be examined across speaker and channel variation, rather than only as undifferentiated figures. That is pertinent to the goal of separating pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation. Stratification can reveal differences across those conditions, but the plan does not state what those differences will be.
Does stratifying by speaker and channel automatically establish the requirement about independently varying speakers and channels?

Not automatically. Stratification describes how the WER results are to be examined. The original requirement also specifies a condition—speakers and channels vary independently—under which the existing-accent WER increase must stay within one percentage point. The plan names speaker/channel-stratified measurements, but it does not supply a result or further details establishing that condition.
Am I comparing the two selection strategies, or comparing each one against the frozen recognizer?

The comparison explicitly planned here is 0.85 filtering versus phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling. Separately, the broader unseen-accent target is defined relative to the frozen recognizer: at least a 15% relative WER reduction using only unlabeled adaptation speech. The plan does not state that either selection condition has met that target.
Could a lower WER with 0.70 sampling answer the original concern even if we cannot tell whether more shifted vowels were retained?

It would support the predicted WER benefit of that sampling condition relative to 0.85 filtering, but it would leave the proposed explanation about discarded shifted-vowel material unresolved. Measuring both retention and WER matters because they answer different parts of the question.
And if shifted-vowel retention increases but unseen-accent WER does not improve?

That would distinguish retaining more shifted-vowel material from obtaining the predicted WER reduction. The plan is capable of examining both, without assuming they must move together. It would not be appropriate to declare that outcome in advance.
Does this plan establish how the accent gate, residual adapters, or disentanglement are implemented?

No. It specifies a comparison between pseudo-label selection conditions on unlabeled AccentShift-12 and the measurements to examine. It does not add an implementation specification for the accent gate, phoneme residual adapters, or adversarial speaker/channel disentanglement.
Can I describe the plan as testing whether sampling to 0.70 solves the whole adaptation goal?

That would overstate it. The plan addresses the cutoff concern by comparing shifted-vowel retention and speaker/channel-stratified WER for unseen and existing accents. The full goal additionally has explicit performance thresholds: at least a 15% relative unseen-accent WER reduction against the frozen recognizer and no more than a one-percentage-point existing-accent WER increase under independently varying speakers and channels. The planned comparison is informative about those concerns, but it does not assume the thresholds will be met.

For this activity, train AccentShift-12 adapters with 0.85 filtering versus phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling, then audit shifted-vowel retention and speaker/channel-stratified WER. What does that encompass?

It encompasses training adapters under the two specified pseudo-label selection conditions on AccentShift-12, then examining two kinds of outcomes: how much shifted-vowel material each condition retains, and word error rate (WER) stratified by speaker and channel. The WER audit covers unseen and existing accents. This describes the activity and its measurements, not findings from it.
Are the two confidence values doing the same job?

They identify the two conditions being compared. One uses 0.85 filtering; the other uses phoneme-balanced sampling down to 0.70. The second condition includes phoneme balance as part of its description, so it should not be reduced to simply applying an unqualified 0.70 filter. No particular sampling rule is specified here.
When you say ‘train adapters,’ do you mean two independently defined adaptation goals?

No. The activity compares how the AccentShift-12 adapters behave under the two pseudo-label selection conditions. Both conditions serve the same broader goal of adapting to an unseen accent while protecting existing-accent recognition. The point of the comparison is to examine the effect of the selection conditions, not to redefine the goal.
Does the activity require labeled AccentShift-12 speech?

No. AccentShift-12 is being used as unlabeled adaptation speech in this comparison. The filtering and sampling conditions concern pseudo-labels, not supplied ground-truth labels for the adaptation speech.
What exactly is being audited when we look at shifted-vowel retention?

The audit concerns how much shifted-vowel material remains under each condition’s pseudo-label selection. It is the direct check on whether the 0.85 filtering condition excludes material associated with the pronunciation shifts the adapters are meant to learn. A retention measurement alone would not tell us whether the retained pseudo-labels are correct or whether WER improves.
If the 0.85 condition excludes at least 40% of shifted-vowel frames, can we treat that number as already established by starting this activity?

No. At least 40% is the hypothesized exclusion, not an established measurement. Auditing shifted-vowel retention is part of examining it. Starting or describing the training and audit does not supply the exclusion fraction.
Does sampling down to 0.70 guarantee recovery of all vowel-shift frames rejected at 0.85?

No. Frames below 0.70 would not be recovered merely by sampling down to 0.70, and the phoneme-balanced condition does not imply that every eligible frame is included. The activity calls for auditing retention precisely because the amount retained cannot be read off from the two confidence values alone.
Why pair the retention audit with a WER audit rather than stopping at retained frames?

Retention addresses whether the training selection preserves shifted-vowel material. WER addresses recognition performance. More retained frames could provide useful pronunciation information, but they could also bring in unreliable pseudo-labels; the retention figure by itself cannot establish the predicted unseen-accent WER benefit.
What does ‘speaker/channel-stratified WER’ mean in the scope of this activity?

It means examining WER with speaker and channel variation kept visible, rather than reporting only an overall figure that combines those conditions. The audit concerns both unseen- and existing-accent WER. This is pertinent because the adaptation goal calls for separating pronunciation shifts from speaker and channel variation.
Could a single overall unseen-accent WER number replace that stratified audit?

Not without losing part of what this activity specifies. An overall unseen-accent number could describe aggregate recognition performance, but it would not show how performance varies across speakers and channels, and it would not cover existing-accent WER. The stated audit explicitly includes those dimensions.
Is this activity also an audit of whether existing accents are protected?

Yes, through the existing-accent portion of the speaker/channel-stratified WER audit. The broader requirement limits existing-accent WER increases to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels. The activity examines relevant WER behavior; it does not assert that the limit has been met.
And for the unseen accent, does carrying out the training mean we have achieved the ≥15% relative WER reduction?

No. Training and auditing are activities, not performance results. The broader target is an unseen-accent WER reduction of at least 15% relative to the frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech. Nothing in this activity states a measured reduction or says that target has been achieved.
Should the WER comparison be read as just 0.85 versus 0.70, or as a claim that one of them beats the frozen recognizer?

Here, the specified training comparison is between 0.85 filtering and phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling. The frozen recognizer defines the broader unseen-accent performance target, but this activity reports no WER values and makes no claim that either condition beats that baseline by any amount.
Can we infer from the word ‘audit’ that a speaker or channel confound has been found?

No. Auditing speaker/channel-stratified WER is a way to look for how recognition performance behaves across those variations. It does not imply that a confound has been detected, that disentanglement has worked, or that any particular stratum performs better or worse.
So what is the most accurate short description of the work at this point?

Train AccentShift-12 adapters under 0.85 pseudo-label filtering and phoneme-balanced sampling down to 0.70, and audit shifted-vowel retention alongside speaker/channel-stratified unseen- and existing-accent WER. The activity examines the proposed trade-off between retaining pronunciation-shift evidence and recognition performance; its outcomes remain to be measured.
What did the AccentShift-12 comparison show for shifted vowels and unseen-accent WER?

On AccentShift-12, 0.85 pseudo-label filtering excluded 44% of shifted-vowel frames. In the adapter comparison, unseen-accent word error rate (WER) was 28.0% with 0.85 filtering and 24.1% with phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling.
What is the WER difference in percentage points?
It is a decrease of 3.9 percentage points: 28.0% minus 24.1%. That is the difference between the two selection conditions in this comparison.
And what is the relative decrease between those conditions?
Relative to the 28.0% WER with 0.85 filtering, the decrease is 3.9 divided by 28.0, or about 13.9%. That uses the 0.85-filtering condition as its reference, not the frozen recognizer.
Is the 44% figure a WER figure too?

No. The 44% describes shifted-vowel frames excluded by 0.85 filtering. The 28.0% and 24.1% figures are unseen-accent WER values, measured at the word level. They answer different questions: what the filter removed and how recognition performed under the two sampling conditions.
Does 44% excluded mean 44% of all AccentShift-12 speech was discarded?
No. The denominator is shifted-vowel frames. The evidence does not give the fraction of all AccentShift-12 speech, all vowel frames, or all pseudo-labels that the 0.85 filter excluded.
Can I say phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling recovered every one of those excluded frames?

No. The evidence reports the exclusion rate at 0.85 and the WER under balanced 0.70 sampling, but it does not report how many of the excluded shifted-vowel frames were included by that sampling condition. In particular, it does not say where all their confidence values fell.
So the WER improvement proves that recovering shifted-vowel frames caused it?

The reported comparison does not isolate that causal explanation. It shows lower unseen-accent WER with phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling than with 0.85 filtering, alongside the finding that 0.85 filtering excluded 44% of shifted-vowel frames. It does not separately establish which additional frames were sampled or how much each contributed to the WER difference.
Should I describe the result as simply lowering the cutoff to 0.70?

That would leave out an important part of the reported condition. The comparison is between 0.85 filtering and *phoneme-balanced* 0.70 sampling. The evidence does not separate the effect of the 0.70 level from the effect of balancing, so the result should be attributed to the condition as described.
Does 24.1% establish the required relative improvement over the frozen recognizer?

The figures here do not provide the frozen recognizer’s unseen-accent WER. The 28.0% comparison value belongs to the 0.85-filtering adapter condition, so the 13.9% relative difference calculated from 28.0% and 24.1% is not a calculation against the frozen recognizer.
What can I say about existing-accent WER from these figures?

These figures report shifted-vowel exclusion and unseen-accent WER only. They do not give existing-accent WER values, including the speaker/channel-stratified values, so they do not quantify any existing-accent WER change.
Do the numbers tell us whether the speaker and channel variation was successfully disentangled?

No. The reported numbers do not describe speaker- or channel-specific performance or directly measure disentanglement. The overall unseen-accent WER decrease should not be treated as a measurement of how well speaker and channel variation was separated from pronunciation shifts.
What is a precise way to state the finding without adding those conclusions?

You could state: ‘On AccentShift-12, 0.85 pseudo-label filtering excluded 44% of shifted-vowel frames. Phoneme-balanced 0.70 sampling yielded 24.1% unseen-accent WER, compared with 28.0% under 0.85 filtering—a decrease of 3.9 percentage points.’ That reports the measured comparison without assigning an unmeasured cause or adding claims about the frozen recognizer or existing accents.

I’d like to propose training a phoneme-level adapter router on augmentation-consistent pronunciation shifts, with speaker/channel-sensitive routing decisions reverting to frozen decoding. How should I explain it?

Present it as a proposed way to decide when pronunciation-focused adaptation is appropriate. The router would make decisions at the phoneme level, using pronunciation shifts that remain consistent under augmentation as its training signal. If a routing decision appears sensitive to speaker or channel variation, the proposal calls for reverting that decision to frozen decoding. This is an intended safeguard, not evidence that the router can yet make those distinctions reliably.
What does the router decide at the phoneme level?

The proposal concerns whether an adapter should be used for a pronunciation-related decision at that level, rather than making only one undifferentiated choice for an entire utterance. It does not specify the router’s architecture, its exact output, or how phoneme-level choices are combined during decoding.
Does that mean the router changes the phonemes themselves?

Not necessarily. ‘Phoneme-level’ describes the granularity of the proposed routing decision. It does not, by itself, specify how phonemes are represented or how the adapter changes recognition. The stated proposal is about directing adapter use and falling back to frozen decoding when a decision is speaker/channel-sensitive.
What qualifies as an augmentation-consistent pronunciation shift?

Conceptually, it is a pronunciation-related pattern that remains stable across augmented views of the speech, rather than appearing only because of one particular view. The proposal does not specify the augmentations, a consistency metric, or a threshold for deciding that a shift qualifies.
Are you saying consistency under augmentation proves a shift is accent-related?

No. Consistency is a proposed signal for training the router, not proof that a pattern reflects accent rather than some other stable property. The proposal still needs the distinction between pronunciation shifts and speaker or channel variation to work in practice.
How does the speaker/channel-sensitive fallback relate to that concern?

It supplies a second safeguard: when a proposed routing decision changes in a way that indicates sensitivity to speaker or channel variation, that decision reverts to frozen decoding instead of relying on the adapter route. The aim is to avoid treating nuisance variation as a reason to adapt pronunciation. The proposal does not define a sensitivity test or claim the safeguard catches every such decision.
Does a speaker/channel-sensitive decision mean the speaker or channel is necessarily the only reason it changed?

No. The phrase identifies decisions that the proposed router would treat as sensitive to those variations; it does not establish a complete causal explanation for any particular decision. How that sensitivity would be identified is not specified here.
Is frozen decoding used for every existing-accent utterance?

The proposal does not state a blanket rule for all existing-accent utterances. It specifically says to revert speaker/channel-sensitive routing decisions to frozen decoding. We should not turn that decision-level safeguard into a claim that every utterance of an existing accent takes the frozen path.
Nor does it say an entire utterance must fall back whenever one phoneme-level decision is sensitive, right?

Right. The proposal names phoneme-level routing decisions and says sensitive decisions revert to frozen decoding. It does not specify whether or how a decision-level fallback affects other decisions within the same utterance.
Why use frozen decoding as the fallback?

It offers a way not to apply an adapter decision when that decision appears tied to speaker or channel variation rather than a pronunciation shift. That aligns with the aim of protecting recognition of existing accents. It remains an intended protection mechanism, not a guarantee about the resulting word error rate.
Would it be fair to say the router is speaker- and channel-invariant?

That would be too strong as a description of the proposal. It aims to train on augmentation-consistent pronunciation shifts and to revert decisions that appear speaker/channel-sensitive. Neither provision establishes that every remaining routing decision is invariant to speakers and channels.
Could the fallback also suppress useful adaptation?

Possibly. If a decision that would have benefited from adapter use is treated as speaker/channel-sensitive, reverting it to frozen decoding could forgo that benefit. The proposal balances a potential protection against the risk of missing useful pronunciation adaptation; it supplies no measurements of either effect.
Is this a proposal to train on labeled adaptation transcripts?

No labeled adaptation transcripts are specified. The broader goal is unsupervised adaptation using only unlabeled adaptation speech. This proposal identifies a training signal—augmentation-consistent pronunciation shifts—but does not spell out how that signal is obtained or add labeled adaptation speech.
Can I claim this router will meet the unseen-accent WER target?

Not from the proposal alone. The target remains an unseen-accent word error rate reduction of at least 15% relative to the frozen recognizer using only unlabeled adaptation speech. A phoneme-level router and its fallback describe a possible approach, not a measured reduction.
And how does it relate to the existing-accent requirement?

Reverting speaker/channel-sensitive decisions to frozen decoding is intended to reduce the risk of harming existing accents. The requirement, however, is quantitative: existing-accent WER increases must be limited to one percentage point under independently varying speakers and channels. The fallback’s presence does not establish that limit.
Does the proposal specify which augmentations to apply, or a score for deciding when to fall back?

No. It specifies augmentation-consistent pronunciation shifts as the training focus and speaker/channel sensitivity as the reason to revert a routing decision. It gives no augmentation recipe, consistency score, sensitivity score, or numerical fallback threshold.
How is this different conceptually from choosing one recognition path for an entire utterance?

The stated granularity is phoneme-level: it proposes making adapter-routing decisions for pronunciation-related parts of speech rather than treating the utterance as a single indivisible routing choice. The exact decoding procedure is unspecified, so that conceptual distinction should not be stretched into a particular implementation.
Could a pronunciation shift be consistent under augmentation while a routing decision remains speaker-sensitive?

Conceptually, yes. Consistency of a proposed pronunciation-shift signal and sensitivity of a routing decision are different considerations. That is why the proposal includes both training on augmentation-consistent shifts and reverting decisions that appear sensitive to speaker or channel variation. It does not state how often that situation occurs.
Would frozen decoding be the comparison baseline as well as the fallback?

Frozen decoding is the proposed fallback for sensitive decisions. Separately, the frozen recognizer is the baseline named in the unseen-accent WER requirement. Those roles should remain distinct: using a fallback does not itself demonstrate an improvement relative to the frozen recognizer.
Can you state the proposal in one sentence without implying it has already worked?

‘Propose training a phoneme-level adapter router on augmentation-consistent pronunciation shifts, while reverting routing decisions that appear sensitive to speaker or channel variation to frozen decoding.’
Does augmentation-consistency gating wrongly reject shifted consonants under mobile compression, eroding unseen-accent WER gains?

That is a possibility, not an established result. If mobile compression makes a genuine shifted-consonant cue look inconsistent across augmented views, the gate could reject a pronunciation-related adapter decision and revert it to frozen decoding. Whether that happens, and whether it raises unseen-accent word error rate (WER), cannot be determined from the question alone.
Why call such a rejection ‘wrong’ if the views really are inconsistent?

It would be wrong relative to the gate’s intended purpose if the underlying pronunciation shift is real and useful for adaptation, but the gate rejects it because compression affects its apparent consistency. Inconsistency in the observed views would not necessarily mean the pronunciation shift itself is absent.
Is mobile compression known to have that effect on shifted consonants here?

No such effect is established by this question. Mobile compression is the condition being examined as a possible source of misleading inconsistency. The question does not report consonant-specific routing decisions or WER under that condition.
Could the gate reject a shifted consonant for a reason unrelated to compression?

In principle, yes. A rejected decision alone would not identify why it was rejected. The question specifically asks whether augmentation-consistency gating misclassifies shifted consonants *under mobile compression*; it does not establish compression as the cause of any rejection.
How does this relate to reverting speaker/channel-sensitive decisions to frozen decoding?

The proposed fallback aims to avoid applying adapters when a routing decision seems sensitive to speaker or channel variation. The concern here is that the safeguard could also reject a genuine pronunciation shift if mobile compression makes that shift appear inconsistent. The same fallback that protects against inappropriate adaptation could, in that case, forgo useful adaptation.
Does a fallback to frozen decoding necessarily add word errors?

No. Its effect depends on how frozen decoding and the adapter path would recognize the affected speech. Even if a shifted-consonant decision were rejected unnecessarily, that would not by itself establish a measurable increase in overall unseen-accent WER.
What does ‘eroding unseen-accent WER gains’ mean precisely?

It means reducing the improvement in unseen-accent WER that adaptation might otherwise deliver. The broader target is at least a 15% relative reduction against the frozen recognizer. This question asks whether rejecting useful shifted-consonant decisions could diminish that improvement; it does not say the target has been missed.
Is the question claiming that all consonant shifts under mobile compression get rejected?
No. It asks whether shifted consonants are wrongly rejected. It supplies no rejection rate, no list of affected consonants, and no claim that every shifted-consonant decision is treated the same way.
Are shifted consonants the same thing as shifted-vowel frames in the pseudo-label filtering discussion?

No. This question concerns whether an augmentation-consistency gate rejects consonant-related pronunciation shifts under mobile compression. Shifted-vowel frame retention concerns which training material passes pseudo-label selection. They involve different pronunciation cues and different selection decisions; a finding about one would not automatically answer the other.
If the gate accepts fewer decisions on mobile speech, does that answer the question?

Not by itself. Fewer accepted decisions would not show that the rejected ones were genuine shifted consonants, that compression caused their rejection, or that the resulting unseen-accent WER gain was eroded. Each of those is part of the concern expressed in the question.
Could augmentation consistency still be useful even if this risk exists?

Yes, conceptually. Consistency can be a useful proposed signal for avoiding decisions driven by variation other than pronunciation. The question probes a potential failure of that signal under mobile compression, not whether every use of augmentation consistency is unsound.
Should I describe this as proof that the phoneme-level router sacrifices unseen-accent performance?

No. The router is proposed, and this question identifies a possible failure mode. Without evidence about shifted-consonant decisions and the resulting WER, it would be premature to say that the router rejects them incorrectly or sacrifices unseen-accent performance.
What would distinguish the routing concern from the WER concern?

The routing concern is whether genuine shifted-consonant decisions are rejected as inconsistent under mobile compression. The WER concern is whether any such rejection reduces the unseen-accent improvement against frozen decoding. One is about the gate’s decisions; the other is about their recognition consequences.
Can you restate the question without assuming its answer?

‘Under mobile compression, does the augmentation-consistency gate reject genuine shifted-consonant pronunciation cues, and, if so, does reverting those decisions to frozen decoding diminish the unseen-accent WER improvement?’

My hypothesis is that compression-aware consistency training should retain at least 80% of shifted-consonant segments on mobile audio while keeping unseen-accent WER at or below 25.5%. How should I state what that predicts?

It predicts two outcomes for mobile audio: retention of at least 80% of shifted-consonant segments, and unseen-accent word error rate (WER) no higher than 25.5%. The idea is that training for consistency with mobile compression in mind may avoid rejecting pronunciation shifts that are useful for adaptation. Both thresholds are hypotheses, not measured results.
What is the denominator in the 80% prediction?
The denominator is shifted-consonant segments on mobile audio. The prediction does not say that 80% of all mobile utterances, all consonants, or all phoneme-level routing decisions will be retained.
Does ‘at least 80%’ mean exactly four out of every five segments must be retained?

No. It is a lower bound on the retention rate for the relevant segments. A rate above 80% would also meet that part of the prediction; the hypothesis does not require the retained segments to be distributed evenly across utterances or consonants.
What does retention mean in relation to the proposed router?

Here it concerns keeping shifted-consonant segments available to the pronunciation-focused adapter-routing approach rather than losing them because a consistency judgment rejects them. The hypothesis does not define a detailed retention rule, so it should not be read as specifying exactly how the router handles every segment.
Does compression-aware consistency training mean we have settled on a particular compression augmentation?

No. It names the proposed training emphasis: consistency should account for mobile compression. The hypothesis does not specify an augmentation recipe, a compression setting, a training objective, or how consistency is measured.
Is the claim that every shift retained will be a genuine pronunciation shift?

No. Retention is not the same as correctness. The ≥80% prediction concerns how many shifted-consonant segments are kept; it does not claim every retained decision is appropriate or that retention alone improves recognition.
Why include a WER ceiling as well as a retention target?

Because keeping more segments is useful only insofar as the resulting recognition performance remains acceptable for the intended unseen-accent task. The hypothesis therefore pairs a segment-level retention prediction with a word-level performance prediction: unseen-accent WER should be no more than 25.5%. Neither quantity determines the other automatically.
Could retention reach 80% while WER exceeds 25.5%?
Yes, in principle. Retaining segments does not guarantee that the routed recognition decisions are accurate. That outcome would meet the retention prediction but not the stated WER prediction.
And could WER be at most 25.5% even if fewer than 80% of those segments are retained?

Yes, in principle. WER summarizes word errors, while the retention rate describes a particular set of shifted-consonant segments. Meeting the WER ceiling would not, by itself, establish the ≥80% retention prediction.

Rather than requiring labeled adaptation transcripts, it would use alternatives represented in ASR lattices from unlabeled speech to infer accent-specific pronunciation variants. For variants judged familiar, the proposal preserves frozen decoding. These are design intentions, not established performance results.
